def: A superficial wound where the skin is scraped away, typically not through the full thickness of the skin.
Having a sudden onset and typically a short, intense course — contrast with chronic.
Without fever; a normal body temperature.
Able to walk.
The relief of pain.
A severe, systemic allergic reaction involving multiple body systems, potentially life-threatening.
Chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle.
The area at the front of the elbow, a common site for IV access and drawing blood.
A medication or measure that reduces fever.
The absence of breathing.
An abnormal buildup of fluid in the abdominal cavity, often from liver disease.
Showing no signs or symptoms of a condition, even if the condition is present.
Impaired coordination or balance, often affecting gait or movement.
Listening to internal body sounds, typically with a stethoscope.
An injury in which a flap or piece of tissue is torn partially or completely away from the body.
Affecting or involving both sides of the body.
An abnormally slow heart rate.
An abnormally slow respiratory rate.
Originating from or caused by the heart, as in cardiogenic shock.
Relating to the head; also used to describe the head-first presentation of a fetus during delivery.
Persisting over a long period of time — contrast with acute.
Skin that is cool and moist to the touch, often a sign of shock or poor perfusion.
The presence of one or more additional conditions alongside a primary condition.
An early stage of shock in which the body's mechanisms (increased heart rate, vasoconstriction) are still maintaining an adequate blood pressure.
A specific situation or condition in which a drug, procedure, or treatment should NOT be used because it could cause harm.
Located on, or affecting, the opposite side of the body.
A bruise — an injury that damages tissue and blood vessels beneath the skin without breaking the skin's surface.
Involuntary, often violent muscle contractions, as seen in a seizure.
A crackling or grating sensation/sound, often from broken bone fragments or air under the skin.
A bluish discoloration of the skin or mucous membranes, typically indicating inadequate oxygenation.
A later stage of shock in which the body's compensatory mechanisms fail, and blood pressure drops — a medical emergency.
Excessive or profuse sweating.
The dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs that is the primary muscle of breathing.
Farther from the point of attachment or the trunk of the body.
Swelling or stretching outward, such as abdominal distention.
Difficulty swallowing.
Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath.
An abnormal heart rhythm; often used interchangeably with arrhythmia.
Bruising — discoloration of skin from blood collecting under its surface.
Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in body tissues.
A blockage in a blood vessel caused by a clot or other material that traveled there from elsewhere in the body.
Vomiting.
Within or through the trachea, as in an endotracheal tube used for advanced airway management.
A nosebleed.
Redness of the skin, often due to inflammation or increased blood flow.
The cause or origin of a disease or condition.
An open abdominal wound severe enough that internal organs protrude through it.
A worsening of a disease or its symptoms.
Severe blood loss to the point of being life-threatening; bleeding out.
The process of freeing and removing a trapped patient, such as from a wrecked vehicle.
Having a fever.
Lacking normal muscle tone; limp.
A seated position with the head of the bed/stretcher raised, often used to ease breathing.
A person's manner or pattern of walking.
Involuntary muscle tensing over a painful area, often the abdomen, to protect it from further pain.
Vomiting blood.
A localized collection of blood outside a blood vessel, often causing swelling.
Weakness affecting one side of the body.
Coughing up blood, typically from the respiratory tract.
Heavy or uncontrolled bleeding.
A collection of blood in the pleural space (between the lung and chest wall).
The body's tendency to maintain a stable, balanced internal environment.
An abnormally high body temperature.
Inadequate blood flow to the body's tissues and organs — another term for shock.
An abnormally low body temperature.
An abnormally low volume of circulating blood/fluid in the body.
A deficiency of oxygen reaching the body's tissues.
Of unknown cause.
A specific situation or condition in which a drug, procedure, or treatment IS appropriate to use.
Tissue death caused by an inadequate blood supply, as in a myocardial infarction.
Developing gradually and subtly, without an obvious sudden onset.
Visually examining a patient or body region.
Located on, or affecting, the same side of the body.
An inadequate blood supply to an organ or tissue, which can progress to infarction if not corrected.
A yellowish discoloration of the skin and eyes, often from liver dysfunction or excess bilirubin.
The study of motion and forces involved in an injury — used to predict likely injury patterns from a mechanism of injury.
An abnormal, exaggerated forward curvature of the upper spine.
A cut or tear through the skin, which may be smooth or jagged.
A state of sluggishness, drowsiness, or reduced responsiveness.
Mentally clear; able to think and communicate normally.
A general feeling of discomfort, illness, or unease.
The central compartment of the chest, containing the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus.
Dark, tarry stool, often indicating upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
A blotchy, patchy discoloration of the skin, often a sign of poor perfusion or impending death.
Widening of the nostrils with each breath, a sign of respiratory distress, especially in children.
The death of body tissue.
A newborn infant, generally within the first 28 days of life.
Involuntary, rhythmic eye movement, which can be a sign of neurological injury or certain intoxications.
A blockage or closure of a passage, such as an airway or blood vessel.
Difficulty breathing while lying flat, relieved by sitting up.
Treatment intended to relieve symptoms and improve comfort rather than cure the underlying condition.
Unusual paleness of the skin, often associated with poor perfusion.
Examining by touch, feeling for abnormalities like tenderness, masses, or crepitus.
A sensation of a rapid, fluttering, or pounding heartbeat.
Movement of a segment of the chest wall in the opposite direction from the rest of the chest during breathing, seen in flail chest.
Paralysis affecting the lower half of the body, typically both legs.
An abnormal sensation, such as tingling, numbness, or "pins and needles."
A microorganism capable of causing disease, such as a virus or bacterium.
Relating to infants, children, and adolescents — generally patients under 18 years of age.
Tapping on a body surface to assess the underlying structure by the resulting sound.
The flow of blood through blood vessels to an organ or tissue, delivering oxygen and nutrients.
Relating to the outer parts of the body, away from the center, such as the peripheral pulses in the wrists and feet.
Small, pinpoint red or purple spots on the skin caused by minor bleeding under the surface.
Unusual sensitivity to light.
A collection of air in the pleural space, causing partial or complete lung collapse.
Excessive thirst.
Excessive urination.
The period immediately following a seizure, typically marked by confusion, drowsiness, or altered mental status.
Occurring or provided before a patient reaches the hospital, i.e. EMS care in the field.
The sensation of nearly fainting, without actually losing consciousness.
A persistent, often painful erection unrelated to sexual stimulation, sometimes seen in spinal injury or certain medical conditions.
Early symptoms that signal the onset of a disease, before more definitive symptoms appear.
A forecast of the likely course or outcome of a disease or condition.
Lying face-down.
Closer to the point of attachment or the trunk of the body.
Itching.
Drooping of the upper eyelid, which can be a sign of a neurological problem such as stroke.
A buildup of fluid in the lungs, often caused by heart failure, that impairs oxygen exchange.
Paralysis affecting all four limbs, typically from a high spinal cord injury.
Abnormal crackling or bubbling lung sounds, often associated with fluid in the airways, such as pulmonary edema.
Pain that occurs (or worsens) when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, suggesting peritoneal irritation.
Coarse, low-pitched, rattling lung sounds, often caused by secretions in the larger airways.
The stiffening of the body's muscles after death — one of several presumptive/definitive signs used to identify obvious death.
The white outer layer of the eyeball.
A life-threatening, dysregulated body response to infection that can lead to organ dysfunction and shock.
A condition resulting from a prior disease or injury.
An objective finding that can be observed or measured by another person, such as a rash or an abnormal pulse — contrast with a symptom.
Immobilizing an injured body part, typically to prevent further injury and reduce pain.
A high-pitched, harsh sound heard on inspiration, indicating a narrowed or partially obstructed upper airway.
Air trapped beneath the skin, producing a distinctive crackling sensation on palpation, often seen with chest trauma.
Lying face-up.
A subjective sensation reported by the patient, such as pain or nausea, that can't be directly observed by someone else — contrast with a sign.
A temporary loss of consciousness, often from a brief drop in blood flow to the brain — fainting.
An abnormally fast heart rate.
An abnormally fast respiratory rate.
A weak, difficult-to-palpate pulse, often associated with poor perfusion or shock.
A ringing, buzzing, or other sound perceived in the ears without an external source.
A seizure type featuring an initial stiffening phase (tonic) followed by rhythmic jerking (clonic).
A characteristic group of signs and symptoms associated with exposure to a particular class of toxin or drug.

A supine position on an incline with the head lower than the feet; the related shock position (legs raised with the body flat) is sometimes called modified Trendelenburg. Historically used for shock (use varies by current protocol).
A posture in which a patient in respiratory distress leans forward, bracing on their arms, to ease breathing.
Sustained, involuntary contraction of the jaw muscles, making it difficult or impossible to open the mouth.
The skin's elasticity, often assessed by pinching it — poor turgor can be a sign of dehydration.
Affecting or involving only one side of the body.
Hives — raised, itchy welts on the skin, often an allergic reaction.
The narrowing of blood vessels, which increases blood pressure and diverts blood flow.
The widening of blood vessels, which decreases blood pressure and increases blood flow to an area.
A sensation of spinning or dizziness, often related to the inner ear.
Capable of living, such as a fetus that has developed enough to survive outside the womb.
A high-pitched, whistling lung sound produced by air moving through narrowed airways, typical of asthma or COPD.
